messages.subject: Compiler/Rcpp/other(?) warnings using Rstan 2.5.0 on Windows 7.
parts:
Hello Stan Users,

I am getting a series or warnings/errors when I try and run analyses using Rstan that I don't understand, and that I haven't been able to fix with the more obvious online suggestions (e.g. http://tonybreyal.wordpress.com/2011/12/07/installing-rcpp-on-windows-7-for-r-and-c-integration/). I suspect it is something pretty simple, but I'm a bit out of my depth, and am hoping I can get some guidance. Please let me know if there is any additional information I can provide to help clarify my problem.

First, I'm running R 3.1.2 on Windows 7 pro, and have downloaded and installed RStan V2.5.0. as per https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started. Although I don't think it is relevant to this error, I have been running R from Emacs via ESS (but I get the same errors whether I run from Rgui or Emacs). I have copied & attached what I hope is all the relevant info to help diagnose the problem. In case it is relevant, here is the end of my Path environment variable: C:\R_home\Rtools\gcc-4.6.3\bin;C:\R_home\Rtools\bin;C:\R_home\batchfiles_0.7-1;C:\R_home\R-3.1.2\bin\x64;...

sessionInfo()

Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)

locale:
[1] LC_COLLATE=English_Australia.1252  LC_CTYPE=English_Australia.1252

The simple stan model I was using to test whether things were working was:
rstanString="
data {
   int<lower=1> n;
   int<lower=1> p;
   matrix [n,p] X;
   vector [n] y;
}
parameters {
   vector[p] beta;
   real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {

   #Priors
   beta ~ normal(0, 100000);
   sigma~ uniform(0,100);

   #Likelihood
   y ~ normal(X * beta, sigma);
}
 writeLines(rstanString,con="vec_reg.stan")



I attempted to run this model with the following dummy data and options:
set.seed(3)
n = 100
intercept = 5
temp = runif(n)
nitro = runif(n) + 0.8 * temp
int.eff = 2
temp.eff <- 0.85
nitro.eff <- 0.5
res = rnorm(n, 0, 1)
coef <- c(int.eff, temp.eff, nitro.eff, int.eff)
mm <- model.matrix(~temp * nitro)
y <- t(coef %*% t(mm)) + res
data <- data.frame(y, x1 = temp, x2 = nitro, cx1 = scale(temp, scale = F), cx2 = scale(nitro, scale = F))
Xmat <- model.matrix(~cx1+cx2, data)
data.list <- with(data, list(y = y, X = Xmat, n = nrow(data), p = ncol(Xmat)))
nChains = 3
burnInSteps = 3000
thinSteps = 5
numSavedSteps = 15000 #across all chains
nIter = ceiling(burnInSteps+(numSavedSteps * thinSteps)/nChains)


And here is my call to stan:
data.rstan <- stan(data=data.list,
           file="vec_reg.stan",
           chains=nChains,
           iter=nIter,
           warmup=burnInSteps,
           thin=thinSteps,
        verbose=TRUE
           )

I have attached the output as a .txt file. I think there are a few things going on. First, I am getting the same old cygwin error that other people have reported (I know there is nothing for you guys to fix here). But after that there is a series of warnings and other reports that I don't understand, and that I would like to go away. But the model runs in the end anyway... so I'm not sure what all the noise is about. Thank you in advance for any and all.

Cheers,
Colin

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Compiler/Rcpp/other(?) warnings using Rstan 2.5.0 on Windows 7.
parts:
I'm not sure what you think is an error. There are a couple compiler
warnings and we're continually trying to silence them, but they're not
a problem.

The warning tagged "Informational message" is informative.
It is indicating that the sampler is running into numerical problems with
the Hamiltonian simulation. This isn't a concern if it only happens once.
You can reduce the number of such warnings at the cost of speed by reducing
initial step size and increasing the acceptance target, both of which keep
the step size down and reduce discretization (numerical) error in the Hamiltonian
dynamics.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Compiler/Rcpp/other(?) warnings using Rstan 2.5.0 on Windows 7.
parts:
Yup --- the compiler warnings can be ignored.

The root cause is that we sometimes code generate variables in the models
through general algorithms that aren't used in particular cases, and those
cause warnings. For example, we generate a single constant 0 value to avoid
autodiff overhead from repeated use, but it only gets used in models with local
real variables. Not being used in other cases is not a problem, it just
gives a compiler warning.

- Bob
